summary: HETA proposes a three-component attribution framework for decoder-only LLMs combining attention-weighted semantic flow, Hessian-based second-order sensitivity, and KL-divergence information loss. The problem is real and consequential, and the multi-component design is motivated with reasonable theoretical grounding. However, the paper's core credibility rests on a self-designed evaluation metric (DSA) whose construction appears tailored to favor the method, on performance margins that are implausibly large (>2x over the next best method), on ground-truth annotations generated by proprietary LLMs, and on missing ablations over the two most important hyperparameters (β and γ). These issues combine to make the empirical claims unreliable rather than merely weak.
strengths: Addresses a genuine and underexplored gap: existing attribution methods are predominantly designed for encoder-only architectures, and the motivation for rethinking them under decoder-only causal masking is well-argued.
The three-component design is principled and the second-order Taylor expansion argument for why first-order methods fail in saturated regimes is mathematically sound and clearly presented.
Broad comparison suite (9 baselines, 4 models spanning 6B–70B) and robustness evaluation across decoding hyperparameter grids are commendably thorough relative to typical ICLR submissions.

Ablation study isolates each component (Transition Only, Hessian Only, KL Only, No Gating, Uniform Transition) and finds consistent incremental gains, supporting the claim that all three components contribute.

key_concerns.issue: The primary novel evaluation metric (DSA) is authored by the same team and its construction—concatenating an unrelated NarrativeQA narrative with a SciQ evidence paragraph—is specifically designed to test exactly the kind of causal gating that is HETA's distinguishing feature. Using a self-designed metric whose structure perfectly mirrors one's own method as a primary evaluation vehicle is a methodological circularity that prevents independent validation of the central claim.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Either (a) include DSA as a secondary analysis only and make Soft-NC/Soft-NS the primary results, or (b) release the curated dataset and DSA implementation pre-submission so that baselines can be evaluated by neutral third parties, or (c) add results on at least one independently published faithfulness metric not used during HETA design (e.g., AOPC, ROAR, comprehensiveness/sufficiency from DeYoung et al. 2020).

key_concerns.issue: The performance margins are implausibly large: HETA achieves Soft-NC of 10.3 on LongRA (GPT-J) vs. ReAgent at ~3.6 and DSA of 4.8–5.1 vs. ReAgent at 3.5–3.78. A >2x improvement over a strong, recent baseline across every model and every dataset is exceptional at this scale; such margins in attribution research are almost always explained by asymmetric implementation quality, hyperparameter tuning favoritism, or metric construction bias. The paper provides no ablation confirming baselines were run with their reported best settings.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Provide a reproducibility table listing each baseline's hyperparameter configuration, software version, and a reference to which published results (if any) those numbers were checked against. If baselines substantially underperform their reported numbers, explain why. Consider adding a sanity-check comparing to the numbers in the original baseline papers on any shared dataset.

key_concerns.issue: Ground-truth token annotations for the curated dataset are generated by GPT-4o and GPT-5 Thinking, then intersected. Using proprietary LLM outputs as attribution ground truth is circular when those same LLMs are used downstream to score F1/DSA alignment, and it introduces unknowable systematic bias into the evaluation. Furthermore, GPT-5 Thinking is an extremely recent model whose internal attribution tendencies are unstudied, making reproducibility of the annotation pipeline uncertain.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Commission human annotations from at least 3 annotators on a stratified random subset (e.g., 200 instances) and report inter-annotator agreement alongside model agreement. Report LLM-only and human-only results separately so readers can judge the reliability of LLM annotations.

key_concerns.issue: The final attribution combines components via β and γ set to 0.5 each with no ablation over these weights. These two hyperparameters directly control the relative importance of the Hessian and KL terms and are the most influential design knobs in the model. Their sensitivity is not reported anywhere in the main paper or appendix references.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add a 2D sensitivity plot (β, γ ∈ {0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9}) for at least one model–dataset combination, and report the β, γ values that maximize Soft-NC on a held-out split used only for tuning (or report that the same values were used for all models without tuning, in which case state this clearly).

key_concerns.issue: Hessian computation for LLaMA-3.1-70B (even restricted to 6 layers with rank-64 low-rank estimation) is almost certainly the most expensive operation in any comparison, yet the paper reports only a qualitative mention of 'higher runtime' without a single concrete wall-clock or FLOP figure. Without timing numbers, the method's practicality claim cannot be evaluated.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Add a runtime and peak-memory comparison table (seconds per instance, GB) for each method × model across the experimental configurations used in Table 3.

key_concerns.issue: The semantic transition component uses target-conditioned attention rollout (Abnar & Zuidema 2020 extended to decoder causal masking), yet the motivation section argues strongly that attention-based methods are fundamentally unreliable because they do not capture causal influence. The paper does not resolve this tension: if attention rollout is an inadequate causal signal by itself, its use as a causal gate for the entire attribution score requires explicit justification.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Discuss this directly: explain in what regime attention rollout is reliable as a causal gate vs. unreliable as a standalone attribution, or provide an ablation showing that replacing the rollout gate with an alternative causal mechanism (e.g., causal scrubbing or activation patching) yields similar results.

key_concerns.issue: Table 3 as it appears in the manuscript has garbled entries: the HETA row values for GPT-J read '10.32.31' and '9.22.04', which suggests the Soft-NC and Soft-NS values have been typeset without column separators, making independent verification of numerical claims impossible. Additionally, the ReAgent row appears to be absent for GPT-J and Phi-3 in Table 3 despite ReAgent being described as the strongest non-HETA baseline throughout the text.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Correct the table formatting and add the ReAgent row for all models.

key_concerns.issue: The abstract and body contain multiple grammatical errors and typesetting artifacts ('quantifyingthe', 'generallyevaluating', 'and however, most existing') suggesting the manuscript was submitted without a final proofreading pass. While not scientifically disqualifying, these reduce the submission's polish below ICLR norms.
key_concerns.suggested_fix: Conduct a full proofreading pass; the abstract especially should be clean.

questions_for_authors: Can you provide the wall-clock time and peak GPU memory for HETA-LR+WIN versus each baseline (ContextCite, ReAgent, SEA-CoT at minimum) per instance on each tested model? The method's practical utility depends on this.

For Table 3, what are the exact Soft-NC and Soft-NS values for HETA on GPT-J and Phi-3 and what are ReAgent's values on the same models? The extracted table appears to have typesetting errors that prevent verification.

The baseline Soft-NC and Soft-NS values for LLaMA-3.1-70B in Table 3 are substantially lower (many < 1.5) than for GPT-J and Phi-3. Is this a known property of larger models, or does it reflect a different experimental configuration for LLaMA? Please clarify.

Why were β = γ = 0.5 chosen, and is this the same value across all four models? If these were tuned on any part of the evaluation data, the tuning procedure needs to be described and a held-out test set identified.

The DSA metric sums attribution mass over 'model-selected important token indices' S_SciQ and S_NarrQA — how is this token selection performed (top-k? threshold?), and is the same selection rule applied identically to all methods?

Given that the Hessian component uses attention rollout as a causal gate, and the paper argues attention rollout is an unreliable causal signal, what justifies using rollout for gating rather than, say, causal intervention (activation patching)?
Can you share at least 20 input–attribution–prediction examples from the curated dataset along with HETA and ReAgent attributions so reviewers can judge calibration qualitatively?
calibration_check: The claim of 'establishing a new standard for interpretability in autoregressive language models' is substantially overclaimed relative to the evidence: the primary novel metric was designed by the authors, the margins are unrealistically large and not validated against independently reported baseline numbers, and no significance tests are provided; the contribution is real but the claimed magnitude of improvement is not yet credibly established.

significance.justification: Token-level attribution for decoder-only LLMs is a genuinely important open problem, and ICLR researchers in interpretability and LLM safety would care about a credible solution, but the current evaluation leaves the actual magnitude of the contribution uncertain.

novelty.justification: Combining attention-value rollout, Hessian-vector products, and KL-masked perturbation into a unified gated score is a new combination, though each individual component is drawn from prior work; the architectural tailoring to decoder causal masking adds modest novelty.

rigor.justification: The theoretical motivation for second-order sensitivity is sound, but the empirical claims depend on a self-designed metric with potentially circular construction, model-generated ground truth, and baselines whose implementation quality is not independently validated.

statistical_soundness.justification: Only 3 seeds are used, standard deviations are reported only informally ('< 0.2', '< ±0.06') without confidence intervals or significance tests, and the β/γ hyperparameter space is not explored despite being central to the method.

calibration_honesty.justification: The abstract and conclusion claim to establish 'a new standard' and 'state-of-the-art', language that is not calibrated to the limitations of a self-designed evaluation metric, model-generated annotations, and unverified baseline parity; the limitations section is brief and focuses only on runtime.

clarity.justification: The method description and motivation are generally readable, but the DSA metric definition has an ambiguous formula presentation in the text extraction, Table 3 has garbled numerical entries, and the abstract contains typesetting errors that should have been caught before submission.

structure_compliance.justification: The paper follows the standard conference structure with appropriate sections; however, substantial experimental results (Qwen model, full ablation, runtime tables) are relegated to appendices in a way that makes the main-paper argument hard to evaluate independently.

reproducibility.justification: Core hyperparameters (β, γ, rank, window size, layer sampling) and hardware (A100 80GB) are specified, but actual runtimes are absent, the curated dataset annotation pipeline depends on GPT-5 Thinking whose API access is not guaranteed, and the table formatting errors make numerical results non-reproducible from the text alone.

related_work.justification: The most relevant recent baselines (ContextCite, TDD, ReAgent, PML, SEA-CoT) are covered and their limitations characterized fairly; the mechanistic interpretability thread is mentioned but only superficially, and some recent attribution-for-generation work from 2024–2025 may be underrepresented.

figure_quality.justification: From captions, Figure 2 (ablation bar plots) and Figure 3 (sensitivity/robustness comparisons with qualitative examples) appear informative and directly tied to the claims; Figure 1 provides a useful conceptual pipeline overview; the captions are sufficiently detailed to judge the display items.

breadth_generality.justification: Four models across 6B–70B and three established benchmarks plus one curated dataset provide reasonable coverage, but all datasets are English QA/biography tasks with factual answers; no code generation, multi-turn, or non-English settings are tested, limiting generality claims.

overall_recommendation.justification: The paper addresses a real and important problem with a principled multi-component design, but the evaluation methodology has serious enough flaws—self-designed metric, model-annotated labels, implausibly large margins, missing hyperparameter sensitivity—that the central empirical claims cannot be accepted at face value without substantial revision and independent validation.
